title: Two-Time World Champion Nikhat Zareen Knocked Out of Commonwealth and Asian Games After Trial Shock
excerpt: A 1-4 loss to Sakshi Chaudhary in Patiala ends Nikhat's multi-sport ambitions and exposes the BFI-SAI turf war that left India's boxers crushed
body:
Nikhat Zareen, India's two-time world boxing champion and one of the country's most decorated combat sports athletes, will not compete at the 2026 Commonwealth Games or the Asian Games after losing 1-4 to Sakshi Chaudhary in the 51 kg selection trials at Patiala. The result marks a stunning reversal for a fighter who, just two years ago, seemed destined to become the face of Indian boxing for a generation.

## What Happened in the Ring

The contest was expected to be competitive; it was not expected to be one-sided. Sakshi Chaudhary — who won gold at the 2023 World Championships and recently moved down a weight class to 51 kg — dominated from the opening bell, winning four of the five rounds on the judges' scorecards. Nikhat, visibly ring-rusty after months on the sidelines, struggled to find her trademark combinations and never established the tempo she needed.

"It's painful," Nikhat said afterwards, her voice steady but her frustration unmistakable. "Athletes got crushed between the SAI-BFI tussle. The last two weeks were torture."

## The BFI-SAI War That Hurt Everyone

Nikhat's defeat cannot be understood without the bureaucratic chaos that preceded it. For months, the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) have been locked in a bitter dispute over selection methodology. SAI had suspended the BFI's assessment-based system — which weighted recent international performances and training data — and mandated a return to traditional open trials.

The abrupt policy shift forced boxers to rapidly adjust their preparation. Fighters who had been training for specific international opponents suddenly found themselves sparring against domestic rivals under unfamiliar selection criteria. Weight cuts were rushed, training camps disrupted, and the mental toll was substantial.

The BFI's preference for a performance-based pathway — which would have likely favoured Nikhat given her world championship pedigree — was overruled. In its place came a trial system that, while more transparent, left several established athletes scrambling.

## India's Boxing Pipeline Under Pressure

Nikhat's absence from two major multi-sport events is a blow to Indian boxing's international ambitions. At 30, she was India's most marketable boxer and a proven medal contender at the highest level. Her omission means India will field a younger, less battle-tested squad in the 51 kg category — a weight class where the competition at both the Commonwealth Games and Asian Games will be fierce.

Sakshi Chaudhary, who advances, is no slouch. Her 2023 world title is a genuine credential, and her willingness to drop weight to 51 kg signals serious intent. But she will need to adjust quickly; the international circuit offers no time for settling in.

The trials also produced other notable results. In the men's draw, Sumit Kundu — making a comeback after injury — defeated Hitesh Gulia to secure his spot on India's squad for both events. His selection adds depth to a men's team that has been inconsistent in recent cycles.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian-origin boxing fans in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada, Nikhat's trials loss resonates on multiple levels. She had become a recognisable figure in diaspora media — her world title victories were covered by Indian-American outlets and celebrated across NRI community platforms. Her absence from the Commonwealth Games, to be held in Glasgow, will be felt acutely by British-Indian fans who had hoped to cheer her in person.

The broader conversation about how Indian sports federations treat their athletes is one that travels easily across borders. NRI sports communities, many of whom follow boxing through platforms like BFI's streaming partnerships and social media, have been vocal about the SAI-BFI dispute — viewing it as emblematic of the institutional dysfunction that often undermines Indian sport.

## What's Next for Nikhat

Nikhat has not announced any retirement plans, and at 30, she has time to rebuild. But the road back is narrow. She will need to compete in BFI-sanctioned events to remain in contention for future selection cycles, and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics — the ultimate prize — will require performances that leave no room for bureaucratic ambiguity.

For now, the ring in Patiala stands as a reminder: in Indian boxing, world titles alone cannot insulate an athlete from the politics that swirl around them.
